transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… what finally pushed me to come in is this thing that happens when I’m driving toward Miami, when my car gets to one of those long bridges. It’s not just that I dislike it or feel a little nervous. The moment I realize I’m on it, my chest tightens right up, and my hands sort of clamp onto the steering wheel like I can’t loosen them.

And then I get this sudden, very strong feeling—almost a certainty—that I have to get off the bridge right then, immediately, even though of course there’s nowhere to go. I know that sounds strange when I say it out loud, because you can’t exactly pull off or turn around, but in that moment it feels urgent, like I have to escape somehow. That’s what made me think I probably shouldn’t keep just trying to handle it on my own.
Is it just bridges that cause this kind of reaction, or are there other situations that make you feel similarly?

It’s mostly those bridges, yes—especially the ones where you’re up there with all that open water around you. I don’t have the same reaction to every ordinary road or anything like that.

And the frustrating part is, I know perfectly well those bridges have been there for years, and thousands of people cross them every day without anything happening. I can tell myself that, and I do tell myself that. But when I think about actually driving over all that open water, the fear just feels so much bigger than the real danger. It’s as if my mind understands it’s probably safe, but my body doesn’t believe it at all.
Do you ever have these intense fear episodes in situations other than when you're driving on a bridge?

Not really in the same way, no. It’s very tied to that situation—being on a bridge, or even thinking about driving onto one, with all that open water around it. I can be perfectly reasonable about it sitting here; I know those bridges have been there forever, and plenty of people drive over them every single day without anything happening.

But when it’s me, and I’m picturing or actually facing that drive, the fear feels completely out of proportion. It’s like the danger in my mind becomes enormous, even though another part of me knows the actual risk is probably small. So no, I don’t get that same intense feeling just anywhere—it’s that bridge situation that does it.
Do you think you've ever had what you would describe as a panic attack, either on a bridge or in any other situation?

I’m not completely sure what would officially count as a panic attack, to be honest. I’ve heard people use that phrase, but I don’t know where the line is between being very frightened and that.

On the bridge, it can feel very sudden and overwhelming, like I need to get out of the situation right away, but I’ve never really stopped afterward and thought, “That was definitely a panic attack.” So I suppose my answer is… maybe? Or I’m not sure. It’s mainly that bridge situation where it gets that intense.
Have you ever had an experience similar to what you described on the bridge in any other situation?

No, not really—not anything that feels like that. What finally made me come in was how immediate it is on those long bridges heading toward Miami. It isn’t even something that builds slowly over an hour or anything. The moment my car reaches one of them, my chest tightens, my hands sort of clamp down on the steering wheel, and I get this sudden, awful certainty that I have to get off the bridge.

And of course that’s the worst part, because there’s nowhere to go. You can’t just pull over or turn around, so I’m sitting there knowing I have to keep driving, but my whole body is acting like I need to escape right then. I don’t really have that same experience in other situations. It’s specifically that bridge, that long stretch, with the water around it.
Have you ever had an experience similar to what you described on the bridge in a situation that doesn't involve driving on a bridge?

No, I really don’t think so. I’ve been trying to think of anything else that comes close, and it keeps coming back to the same thing: those long bridges going toward Miami.

What finally pushed me to come in is that it happens so immediately. The moment my car gets onto one of those bridges, my chest tightens, my hands clamp down on the steering wheel, and I get this sudden feeling—this certainty, almost—that I have to get off. But of course I can’t, because there’s nowhere to go once I’m on it.

I don’t get that in the grocery store, or at home, or just riding around normal streets. It’s that exact situation: being on the bridge, stuck there, with the water around me.
Do you find yourself avoiding driving on bridges because of the fear you experience?

Yes… yes, I have. More than I like to admit, actually. I’ve started arranging my life around whether I’ll have to cross those bridges, which sounds so silly when I say it out loud, but it’s true.

I’ve turned down gallery openings I really would have enjoyed, and birdwatching trips too—things I used to look forward to and plan for. And even visits with my daughter, which is the part that makes me feel the worst. I’ll find myself thinking, “Well, maybe I’ll go another time,” or I’ll only go if someone else can drive me over the bridge.

That embarrasses me. I’ve always been the one who managed things, who made the plans and handled the driving and kept everything moving. So needing someone else to take over just because of a bridge… it makes me feel ashamed, honestly. But yes, I do avoid it when I can.
Is it something about the height of the bridge, the water below, or something else about the bridge itself that triggers your fear, or is it more about the act of driving on it?

It’s… it’s hard to separate, honestly, because it’s the driving and the bridge together. I don’t think it’s just the height, like I’m afraid to look down from a tall building or something. And I know, rationally, those bridges have been there for years. Plenty of people go over them every single day without anything happening.

But when I think about being the one driving over all that open water, with this long stretch ahead of me, the fear just becomes so much bigger than the actual danger. I can tell myself, “This is a normal road, cars are crossing it all day,” but it doesn’t seem to matter much once I’m imagining being out there on it. It’s the open water and the feeling of being stuck driving across it, I think. That combination is what gets to me.
Has your fear of driving on bridges been present for more than six months?

Yes, it has. It’s been about eleven months now, I think—close to a year, anyway. It started around the time my daughter’s heart condition meant she had to begin going down to Miami regularly for specialist visits.

Before that, I can’t remember bridges being something I organized my life around like this. But once those trips became more frequent, and I knew I’d have to deal with those long bridges over the water, it just… became this whole thing. So yes, definitely more than six months.
Would you feel the same level of fear if you were crossing the bridge as a passenger, not driving?

I think… maybe a little less, if I weren’t the one driving, because then I wouldn’t have my hands on the wheel and feel responsible for keeping the car steady. But I don’t think it would disappear, no.

It’s really the thought of being out there over all that open water. I know perfectly well those bridges have been there for years, and people cross them every day without a second thought. I can say that to myself very logically. But when I picture actually being on the bridge, whether I’m driving or even just sitting there, the fear feels much bigger than the actual danger. Like my mind understands one thing, but my body reacts as if it’s something terribly unsafe.

So as a passenger, I might feel slightly better, especially if it’s someone I trust driving. But I’d still be frightened. The bridge and the water underneath it are still there, and I’d still be stuck having to get across.
Would your fear of the bridge be significantly reduced if you were to cross it by a different means, such as walking or taking a bus?

I don’t think it would be significantly reduced, no. Maybe if I weren’t the one actually steering, there might be a small difference, but the main thing is still that I’m crossing that bridge over all that open water.

I know perfectly well those bridges have been there for years, and plenty of people cross them every day without anything happening. I can tell myself that over and over. But when I picture being out there—whether it’s in a car, on a bus, or some other way—the fear just feels much bigger than the actual danger. It’s like the facts don’t quite reach the frightened part of me. Walking might even make me feel more exposed, honestly, but the basic fear is still the bridge and all that water underneath.
Would your fear of the bridge be the same if someone else was driving you across it, but you were still in the car?

Not the same, no—at least I don’t think it would be exactly the same. If someone else were driving, especially someone I trust, I might feel a little less responsible, you know, because I wouldn’t be the one trying to keep the car steady and stay in the lane.

But the fear would still be there in a very real way. It’s the bridge itself, and being out over all that open water. I know, rationally, those bridges have been there for years, and plenty of people drive across them every single day without anything happening. I can tell myself that, and part of me believes it. But when I imagine actually being on it, even just sitting in the passenger seat, the fear feels much bigger than the actual danger. It’s like my body doesn’t care what my mind knows.

So someone else driving might take the edge off a little, but no, it wouldn’t make me comfortable. I’d still be frightened until we were off the bridge.
Would your fear of the bridge be significantly reduced if you were driving on it in a professional driving setting, such as a driving school or under the supervision of a professional?

I don’t think it would be significantly reduced, no. I mean, having a professional there might make me feel a little more reassured in one sense, because I’d think, well, this person knows what they’re doing, they’re used to helping people drive. But the main fear isn’t really about whether I technically know how to drive or whether someone is supervising me.

It’s the bridge itself. It’s being out there over all that open water. I know perfectly well those bridges have been there for years, and plenty of people cross them every day without anything happening. I can tell myself that very clearly, and I do. But when I think about actually driving over it, the fear feels much bigger than the real danger. It’s almost like the logical part of me is saying, “This is safe enough,” but the frightened part of me just doesn’t accept it.

So even in a driving school situation, or with a professional sitting there, I think I’d still be very afraid until I was across. Maybe a little steadier because someone was there, but not enough that I’d say the fear was greatly reduced.
Would your fear of the bridge be present if you were to simply stand on the bridge, not driving or moving, but just standing there?

Yes, I think it would be present. Maybe the driving part adds something, because when I imagine driving I’m thinking about keeping control of the car and not swerving or panicking, but honestly, just standing there on the bridge would still frighten me.

It’s that feeling of being over all that open water. I know perfectly well those bridges have been there for years, and people cross them every day without anything bad happening. I can say that to myself, and I know it’s true. But when I put myself there in my mind—standing on it, looking out, knowing the water is underneath—the fear feels much bigger than the actual danger. It doesn’t feel like my reaction matches what I logically know.

So no, it isn’t only the act of driving. Driving is one version of it, but the bridge itself, being on it over the water, that’s what really sets it off.
Would your fear of the bridge be triggered if you were to see a picture of the bridge, without actually being on it?

A picture would bother me some, I think, but it’s not the same as actually being there. If I see a photo of one of those long bridges, especially if it shows the water stretching out on both sides, I can feel myself tense up a little and I start imagining what it would be like to be on it.

But the real fear—the part that finally made me come in—is when my car actually reaches one of those long bridges toward Miami. It happens right away, almost the moment I’m on it. My chest tightens, my hands clamp down on the wheel, and I get this sudden, awful certainty that I have to get off the bridge, even though of course there’s nowhere to go. I know that sounds unreasonable, because it’s not like anything has changed in that instant, but my body reacts as if I’m in danger.

So a picture can remind me of it, yes, but it doesn’t trigger it the same way as being on the bridge itself.
Would your fear of the bridge be the same if you were a passenger in a car driven by someone else you trust?

I think it might be a little different if I were a passenger with someone I really trusted, because I wouldn’t have to be the one holding the wheel and trying to keep myself steady. But I don’t think the fear would just go away.

What finally made me come in is that when my car reaches one of those long bridges toward Miami, it’s almost immediate. My chest tightens, my hands clamp onto the wheel, and I get this sudden, very strong feeling that I have to get off the bridge right then, even though there’s nowhere to go. If someone else were driving, maybe my hands wouldn’t be on the wheel, of course, but I think that same panic about being on the bridge would still come up.

So no, I don’t think being a passenger would make it the same as riding on a normal road. I might feel a bit safer with someone I trust, but the bridge itself would still trigger that fear.
Would seeing the bridge from a distance, before you're on it, trigger the same fear response as being on the bridge itself?

Seeing it from a distance can start it a little, because I know what’s coming, but it’s not the same as actually being on it.

The thing that really made me come in is what happens the moment my car reaches one of those long bridges toward Miami. It’s like my body reacts before I can talk myself out of it. My chest tightens, my hands clamp onto the wheel, and I suddenly feel absolutely certain that I have to get off the bridge right then—even though there’s nowhere to go.

From a distance, I might get tense or start dreading it, but the full fear doesn’t really hit until I’m actually on the bridge.
Would your fear of the bridge be the same if you were to cross it on foot, without any vehicle?

I don’t really know if it would be exactly the same on foot, because the thing I’ve been dealing with is in the car. What finally made me come in was what happens right when my car gets onto one of those long bridges going toward Miami. It’s almost immediate—my chest tightens, my hands grip the wheel so hard, and I get this sudden feeling like I have to get off the bridge right then, even though there’s nowhere to go.

If I were walking, I suppose the wheel wouldn’t be part of it, obviously, but I imagine the being stuck out there on the bridge would still be the part that scares me. But I can only really tell you what happens in the car, because that’s where it’s been happening.
Would your fear of the bridge be present if you were to cross it by any means other than driving?

I think it probably would still be there, yes, though driving is the way I usually imagine it and the way I’ve actually faced it. It’s not only the mechanics of driving, if that makes sense. It’s the idea of being out there on those long bridges with all that open water around me.

And I do know, rationally, that those bridges have been there for years. People cross them every single day, all day long, and nothing happens. I can tell myself that. But when I picture myself going over all that water, however I’m getting across, the fear feels so much bigger than the actual danger. It’s like my common sense is still there, but it gets drowned out by this feeling that the bridge is unsafe or that I shouldn’t be there.

So I suppose the fear wouldn’t depend completely on driving, but driving is where it really comes up for me.
